overview: Infosys is one of India's largest IT services companies, providing business consulting, technology, digital engineering and business process management services to enterprise clients worldwide, with over four decades of experience and roughly 328,000 employees across 290 locations in 59 countries. It operates a global offshore-centric delivery model (about 77% offshore effort), billing clients on a mix of time-and-materials and fixed-price contracts rather than selling owned products, and now frames its strategy around helping clients build and scale AI ('AI-first' and 'AI-augmented' services) via its Topaz platform. Revenue is concentrated by geography (North America ~55-56%, Europe ~32%) and by industry vertical (Financial Services ~28%, Manufacturing ~16%), and its NSE/BSE-listed equity shares also trade as ADSs on the NYSE under INFY; financial statements are prepared under IFRS in US dollars even though the stock trades in INR.

business_model.summary: Infosys sells labor-intensive technology and consulting services on an engagement/project basis -- application development and maintenance, digital transformation, cloud and data engineering, cybersecurity, consulting, and business process management (BPM) -- billed mostly on time-and-materials or fixed-price contracts, supplemented by smaller software products/platforms revenue (e.g., Finacle, EdgeVerve). A large majority of revenue is 'repeat business' (from clients served in the prior fiscal year as well), giving it quasi-recurring characteristics, but individual engagements are typically singular/project-based rather than subscription-like, so the company must continuously win new work. AI is increasingly embedded as both a growth driver (AI-first services, ~10.5% of Q2 FY2027 revenue) and a margin/pricing risk (AI-augmented productivity commitments compress billing rates).

revenue_streams.name: Others (incl. India, Japan, China, Public Services)

business_model.customer_type: B2B enterprise -- large global corporates and government agencies; FY2026 had 2,060+ active clients, 1,048 'million-dollar' clients and 42 clients each contributing over $100m in LTM revenue; top 5 clients ~12.2% and top 10 ~19.8% of revenue (concentration risk but diversifying)
business_model.geographic_mix: North America ~54.6%, Europe ~32.5%, Rest of World ~10.1%, India ~2.8% (Q2 FY2027); broadly consistent with FY2026 full-year mix of North America 56.1%, Europe 32.1%, RoW 8.9%, India 2.9%

competitive_position.market_position: Second-largest India-based IT services exporter by revenue after TCS, and among the top five global IT services firms by market cap; positions itself as an 'AI-first' navigator of enterprise transformation and claims to be the fastest-growing major IT services brand globally

moat_factors.description: 328,000+ employees, 290 locations/59 countries, ~77% offshore effort ratio gives durable cost advantage versus Western-headquartered consulting rivals (Accenture, IBM)

Large, multi-year outsourcing and application-management contracts and deep knowledge of client systems create stickiness; majority of revenue is 'repeat business', though engagements are formally project-based with no long-term lock-in
Four-decade track record, large deal pipeline ($5.2bn TCV in Q2 FY2027, 62% net new) and recognized quality/process credentials (e.g. CMMI, ISO) support win rates against niche entrants

Finacle (core banking), EdgeVerve, and the Topaz/Topaz Fabric agentic-AI suite provide differentiated, higher-margin offerings versus pure labor arbitrage, though platform revenue remains a small share of the business

50+ partnerships across hyperscalers, AI model developers and enterprise software vendors, plus engagement with ~90% of top 200 clients on AI journeys, position Infosys as a channel for enterprise AI adoption

weaknesses: Commoditized, highly competitive labor-based service model with low pricing power -- clients routinely expect efficiency gains/volume discounts as relationships mature
Heavy dependence on US/UK/EU IT spending cycles and discretionary project budgets, which are the first to be cut in a slowdown
AI threatens to directly substitute for traditional application development/maintenance revenue (its largest historical service lines), forcing Infosys to cannibalize its own base business
Visa/immigration dependence for onsite delivery in the US and Europe exposes the model to policy shocks (e.g., the 2025 $100,000 H-1B fee proclamation)
Smaller scale and narrower consulting/industry breadth than Accenture, which can win larger strategy-led, higher-margin transformation mandates

growth_drivers: AI-first and AI-augmented services -- management estimates an incremental USD 300-400 billion AI-first services opportunity by 2030, with AI already ~10.5% of Q2 FY2027 revenue and rising quarter over quarter
Large deal wins -- $5.2bn of large-deal TCV in Q2 FY2027 (62% net new), including deals over $2bn, following $14.9bn of large-deal TCV in FY2026
Topaz/Topaz Fabric and EdgeVerve platforms monetizing proprietary IP and agentic AI orchestration rather than pure headcount-based billing
Vertical diversification into Energy/Utilities, Life Sciences and Communications, offsetting softness in Retail, Hi-Tech and Manufacturing
Capital-light localization strategy (expanding delivery hubs outside India, e.g., US/Europe near-shore centers) to mitigate visa and tariff risk while capturing 'local-for-local' demand
Capital return program (~85% of cumulative 5-year free cash flow via dividends and buybacks) supporting EPS even in a low-growth revenue environment

business.description: Top 5 clients ~12.2% and top 10 ~19.8% of FY revenue; loss of a major client or large contract could materially affect results
Clients' own in-house AI tools, GCCs, or AI-native competitors could reduce demand for traditional application development/maintenance and BPM services, compress pricing and shrink addressable market
Large global consulting firms, India-based peers, niche AI-native entrants and clients' own Global Capability Centers compete for the same engagements, pressuring win rates and margins
Most engagements are singular in nature; Infosys must continuously win new work rather than relying on contracted recurring revenue
Ongoing Cognizant/TriZetto trade-secret misappropriation lawsuit (filed August 2024) seeking damages and an injunction

financial.description: Revenue is earned mainly in USD/GBP/EUR while a large cost base (wages) is in INR; currency volatility affects margins and the USD value of dividends for ADS holders
India phased out open-market buybacks (effective April 2025) and changed buyback tax treatment, constraining the most EPS-accretive capital return method

financial.risk: SEZ tax benefit step-down and Indian tax policy (GAAR, transfer pricing)
financial.description: Expiring Special Economic Zone tax holidays and potential adverse changes to Indian/foreign tax law could raise the effective tax rate
Past IFRS impairment charges on acquired intangibles; further write-downs possible if acquisitions underperform

regulatory.description: The US Department of Justice is investigating how Infosys classified certain H-1B visa-recipient employees in immigration filings; outcome and potential financial/reputational impact are unknown. Follows a 2013 settlement where Infosys paid $34 million over immigration violations

A September 2025 US presidential proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B applications, tighter Green Card filing rules, and suspension of Infosys (among eight firms) from the Permanent Labor Certification program directly raise onsite delivery costs and constrain staffing flexibility
The EU AI Act and emerging AI rules in other jurisdictions could raise compliance costs and restrict deployment of AI-enabled offerings

regulatory.risk: Indian corporate/securities regulation and sanctions compliance
regulatory.description: SEBI Takeover Code, Companies Act disclosure requirements, and client-sanctions screening add compliance complexity, particularly given clients operating in conflict zones

macro.description: 56% of revenue from North America and 32% from Europe makes Infosys highly sensitive to any slowdown, inflation, or high-interest-rate environment that causes enterprise clients to cut discretionary technology budgets
Conflicts in Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and India-Pakistan tensions can disrupt delivery, divert client budgets to business continuity, and reduce discretionary technology spend
Management explicitly flags risk from new tariffs or taxes on cross-border IT services as a potential direct cost or demand headwind
Competition for AI and digital talent increases wage costs faster than pricing can be passed through to clients

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global IT services spending growth has slowed to low single digits amid cautious discretionary spending, while enterprise AI adoption is reshaping demand toward agentic AI, cloud modernization and outcome-based pricing; Infosys itself cut FY2027 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to 1-2% (from 1.5-3%) after Q2 FY2027 results, reflecting a soft demand environment
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high -- revenue is tied to enterprise discretionary IT budgets which contract in recessions/uncertainty, though a 'repeat business' base and multi-year large deals provide some cushion
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Indirect but meaningful -- higher rates in the US/UK/EU dampen client capital spending and technology budgets; direct balance-sheet sensitivity is low given a net-cash position
key_input_costs: Skilled technology labor (wages, onsite vs. offshore mix)
AI compute and third-party AI model/licensing costs

recent_developments.event: Revenue of $5.145bn, up 1.2% QoQ / 1.5% YoY in constant currency; operating margin held at 21.0%; net profit of $817m (-2.5% YoY in USD, +8.7% YoY in INR terms); AI revenue rose to 10.5% of total revenue from 8.2% in Q1; large deal TCV of $5.2bn (62% net new); FY2027 constant-currency revenue growth guidance cut to 1-2% from 1.5-3%, with operating margin guidance maintained at 20-22%
FY2027 guidance initially trimmed to 1.5-3% constant-currency growth; company announced a CEO succession plan

Salil Parekh, CEO since 2018, to step down around April 2027; Ashiss Kumar Dash (31-year company veteran) named CEO-designate; Nitin Paranjpe appointed non-executive Vice Chairman (May 2026) to strengthen governance and strategic oversight

Interim dividend of ₹26/share declared (record date Nov 3, 2026, up from ₹23 a year earlier); FY2025/26 total shareholder payout (dividends + completed ₹18,000 crore buyback at ₹1,800/share) equaled 113.9% of free cash flow, drawing some shareholder criticism at the AGM over buyback usage

US DOJ confirmed ongoing investigation into Infosys's classification of certain H-1B visa-recipient employees in immigration filings, disclosed as a material government investigation in quarterly filings; outcome still unresolved

US policy headwinds intensified: a presidential proclamation imposed a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa applications, USCIS restricted in-country Green Card filings, and Infosys was among eight firms suspended from the US Permanent Labor Certification program (announced Oct 2026)
Major brokerages (JPMorgan, Citi, UBS, Goldman Sachs, Jefferies) cut price targets following the Q1 FY2027 guidance trim; consensus rating on the US-listed ADS is broadly 'Hold'
Cognizant/TriZetto trade-secret misappropriation lawsuit against Infosys remains in litigation in the US District Court, Northern District of Texas

items.notes: Cut from the 1.5-3% range set after Q1 FY2027 (itself already trimmed from an initial 1.5-3.5% outlook given in April 2026), reflecting softer discretionary spend, especially in Retail and Hi-Tech
Q2 FY2027 operating margin came in at 21.0%, flat QoQ and YoY, within the guided band despite revenue growth pressure

items.target: ~85% of cumulative free cash flow over a rolling 5-year period
items.notes: Delivered via semi-annual dividends and/or buybacks/special dividends; FY2026 actual payout (dividends plus completed buyback) was 113.9% of FCF

items.target: No formal numeric target disclosed, but trend highlighted as a key KPI
items.notes: AI revenue grew from 8.2% of total revenue in Q1 FY2027 to 10.5% in Q2 FY2027; management frames this as the primary growth and investor-relations metric going forward

guidance.management_commentary: Management described Infosys as 'the preferred AI strategy and deployment partner' for its top clients and pointed to $5.2bn of large-deal TCV (62% net new) as evidence of a healthy pipeline, even as it lowered full-year revenue growth guidance for the second consecutive quarter. CFO commentary attributed the cut to continued softness in discretionary spending in segments such as Retail and Hi-Tech, partially offset by growth in Energy/Utilities and Life Sciences, while reaffirming the 20-22% operating margin band and the multi-year capital return policy.

bull_case: Early and credible positioning in enterprise AI services (Topaz/Topaz Fabric, AI playbooks, ~90% of top 200 clients already engaged on AI) could let Infosys capture a disproportionate share of a market management sizes at $300-400bn by 2030
Strong large-deal pipeline ($5.2bn TCV in Q2 FY2027, majority net-new) suggests demand resilience even as organic growth guidance has been cut, providing visibility into future revenue

Disciplined operating margin management (held at 20-22% despite growth deceleration) and a net-cash balance sheet support a generous, policy-driven capital return program (~85% of 5-year FCF) that cushions total shareholder return even in a low-growth year

Offshore-heavy, scaled delivery model (77% offshore effort, 328,000+ employees) retains a structural cost advantage versus Western consulting majors, supporting share gains in cost-takeout engagements during client budget tightening
Diversification into faster-growing verticals (Energy/Utilities, Life Sciences, Communications) is partially offsetting weakness in Retail/Hi-Tech/Manufacturing, broadening the growth base
bear_case: FY2027 constant-currency revenue growth guidance has now been cut twice in two consecutive quarters (3.5% to 3% to 1-2%), signaling a genuinely weak discretionary IT spending environment with limited visibility on recovery

Generative/agentic AI is a double-edged sword: it is simultaneously the industry's main growth narrative and a direct substitute for the labor-based application development/maintenance and BPM services that still constitute the bulk of Infosys's revenue, raising long-term structural margin and growth risk

Unresolved US Department of Justice investigation into H-1B visa-classification practices, compounded by a $100,000 H-1B application fee, tightened Green Card rules, and suspension from the Permanent Labor Certification program, creates binary regulatory/reputational risk concentrated in Infosys's largest market (North America, ~55% of revenue)

Client and revenue concentration (top 10 clients ~20% of revenue) combined with 'singular' project-based engagements means revenue can swing quickly if large clients delay, insource, or build out their own Global Capability Centers

Heavy and rising shareholder payout (113.9% of FCF in FY2026 including buybacks) alongside tightened Indian buyback rules (open-market buybacks phased out from April 2025) limits flexibility and could pressure the balance sheet or dilute capital available for AI platform investment if growth does not reaccelerate
